Note: A minced form of God's blood. Wiktionary notes people swore by Christ's body to dodge the commandment against taking God's name in vain.
Etymology: Oath, from "God's blood".

Note: Wiktionary's 'un is a different word: a form of one without the w (as in 'a good 'un'). It has no entry for the pronoun 'un, him, from Old English hine, so that claim is untested.
Etymology: The reduced pronoun 'un (as in "hit 'un") is from Old English hine.

Note: Acquaintance comes through Old French acointier, to make known, from a Late Latin form of cognoscere, to get to know: the root of cognition and recognise. It names knowing someone over time, not any feeling about them.
Etymology: OF acointance, from acointier "to make known," from L. ad- + cognitus (known) — same root as cognition, recognise. Acquaintance is a form of knowledge, not feeling — it claims what can be shown (they knew each other, over time) without claiming what can't (what either side felt about it).

Note: Adams is Adam plus a patronymic -s. Adam comes via Latin and Greek from Hebrew adam, man, linked to adamah, red earth or ground: the man made of soil.
Etymology: Adams is a patronymic — "son of Adam" — and Adam is Hebrew ādām, man, from ădāmâ, ground or earth. It isn't a name so much as a common noun: the earth-creature, the one made of soil. Which is why it's everywhere. A surname meaning "son of the man made from the ground" was never going to identify anybody in particular — and a man of that name taking an allocation at an enclosure of common ground is a coincidence the language set up long before either of you got there.

Note: From Latin adulterare, to defile or counterfeit, built from ad- and alter, other. Wiktionary glosses the literal sense as going after someone else, not making other, so the defiling sense is confirmed but the gloss is not.
Etymology: From Latin adulterare, "to corrupt, defile," itself from ad- + alter ("other") — literally "to make other," to falsify a thing by mixing in what doesn't belong. The word carries exactly the series' argument in miniature: purity as a category is defined by drawing a boundary around what counts, and adulteration is what that boundary makes visible. Enclosure is the legibility of boundaries; adulteration is what those boundaries create as their opposite.

Note: Wiktionary has afternoon as after- plus noon, with no adjective meaning slow or behindhand. The Surrey sense needs Leveson Gower's glossary.
Etymology: As an adjective, documented Surrey dialect: late, behindhand, slow.

Note: From Greek agōnia, a contest or struggle, from agōn. The death-struggle sense dates from the 1540s and 'extreme pain' only from c.1600, so in 1589 agony still meant a struggle. The source says contest, not specifically wrestling.
Etymology: Greek agōnia, a struggle for victory, specifically wrestling.

Note: The same Latin emendare, but via Old French amender, and the source of mend. Wiktionary gives no date, so the early 13th century needs Etymonline.
Etymology: Early 13th century.

Note: From French or New Latin, from Greek anakhronismos, referring to the wrong time, from khronos, time. Wiktionary gives no dates; the 1640s and the 1816 modern sense need Etymonline.
Etymology: 1640s; the modern sense (thing out of its time) by 1816.

Note: Wiktionary has Scots anerly as an obsolete word for only. 'Solitary' and 'lonely' are not given, and the Sanderson naming story is not tested.
Etymology: From Scots anerly = solitary, lonely; named by William Sanderson, first buyer at the 1827 enclosure auction.

Note: From Latin anxietas, from angere, to distress, akin to Greek ankhō, to choke. The c.1520 arrival date is not on the page.
Etymology: Latin angere "to choke, squeeze"; Greek ankhein; entered English c.1520.

Note: Archive comes via French and Late Latin from Greek arkheion, a magistrate's office, from arkhe, beginning or authority. The office and the authority are confirmed; arkheion itself means belonging to an office, not literally first place.
Etymology: Archive is from Greek arkheion, a magistrate's office, literally "beginning" or "first place," from arkhe — origin, rule, authority. An archive is where power begins — not because of conspiracy, but because power is what decides what's worth writing down.

Note: Arrive comes from Old French ariver, from a medieval Latin verb meaning to come ashore, built on ripa, a riverbank. It was a boat's word before it was a traveller's.
Etymology: OF ariver, from VL arripare, "to come to shore" — ad- (to) + ripa (shore, bank). The original body is entirely about water and edges — a boat reaching land. By Middle English it's landlocked, generalised to any journey's end. Buried in it: the assumption that arriving means crossing a boundary from one medium into another.

Note: From Latin auditus, a hearing. Wiktionary says the checking sense comes from accounts once being presented aloud to an examiner who listened.
Etymology: L. auditus, past participle of audire (to hear) — originally "a hearing" or "an account heard aloud." An audit is something that was said or recounted aloud.

Note: A partial calque of Italian bancarotta, broken bench. Wiktionary links it to a failed moneylender's bench being physically broken.
Etymology: From Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench': the moneylender's counter, physically smashed when he defaulted. The word for the collapse of French royal credit in 1789 literally means the same violent gesture the Crooked Billet hearings performed on the commoners' oral claims — an object destroyed to make a status irreversible.

Note: Wiktionary gives bar from Old French barre, a beam, gate or barrier, from Vulgar Latin barra, of uncertain origin. It gives no Old Norse source: the barrier sense is right, the language is wrong.
Etymology: From Old Norse barr, originally a stick or rod used as a barrier or gate. Became the legal sense ("bar" as legal obstruction, what a lawyer stands behind) and eventually "a standard or threshold." The word's history is about drawing a line something either crosses or doesn't.

Note: Romani beng, the Devil, is inherited from Sanskrit vyaṅga, spotted or frog. Wiktionary records it in Vulcanius's 1593 word list, a continental source, and English and Welsh Romani both use it for the Devil. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: the Devil.

Note: From Hebrew bəʿûlâ, married (of a woman), the name Isaiah gives the land in 62:4; Puritans took it up as a given name.
Etymology: Hebrew, from Isaiah, meaning "married"; land no longer forsaken.

Note: Two different words share one spelling. The log is Old French billette, from bille, a tree trunk, probably Gaulish; the soldier's lodging is Anglo-Norman billette, a list, from Latin bulla, a document.
Etymology: Billet, in the Crooked Billet, is from Old French billette, diminutive of bille — a log, a stick, from a Gaulish root for tree-trunk. The bent branch was a waymarker through the wood. The same word gave English the soldier's billet, a lodging, via an entirely separate route: a billet was also a short written note, from Latin bulla, a seal — hence the written order assigning a soldier to a house. Two words that look identical, one from a piece of wood in a forest and one from a wax seal on a document. The pub kept the wood. The 1827 hearings held inside it turned on the fact that the commoners' rights existed only in the first sense — spoken, marked on the ground, unsealed — and so were refused a hearing.

Note: Bote is Old English bōt, help, remedy or compensation, and 'to boot' comes straight from it. Better is not its descendant: Wiktionary gives better its own line from Old English betera, and lists bōt among its relatives. They are cousins.
Etymology: bote/boot: the Old English word for estovers is the ancestor of better and the phrase 'to boot'; scillingas to bote = shillings as compensation. Project struck: bote is a cognate of better, not its ancestor.

Note: Old English brocc, badger, plus lēah, a woodland clearing.
Etymology: Old English brocc (badger) + lēah (clearing).

Note: Via Latin from Greek kharaktēr, from kharassō, to engrave: a stamped mark before it was a person. The 'pointed stake' link is not on the page.
Etymology: Greek kharaktēr "engraved mark", from kharax "pointed stake".

Note: From Old French charme, chant or magic spell, from Latin carmen, song or incantation. The c.1300 and mid-15th-century dates are not on the page.
Etymology: Latin carmen "song, verse, incantation", from canere "to sing"; entered English c.1300 as incantation; "pleasing quality" mid-15th c.

Note: Wiktionary's main entry, ćhavo, means specifically a Romani boy or son, from Prakrit chāva, a young animal, from Sanskrit. The 17th-century attestation in English Romani is not tested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: boy, child, son; attested in English Romani by the 17th century.

Note: Middle English colier, earlier coler, one who makes or sells charcoal, from Old English col. A collier burned wood long before he dug coal, hence Colliers Wood.
Etymology: From Anglo-Saxon col, charcoal not coal; a charcoal burner, not a coal miner (hence Colliers Wood, first recorded 1632, and Colliers Water Lane).

Note: Wiktionary cites the 'ordinary or vulgar' sense in Shakespeare's Henry VI, written in 1591, long before the parliamentary enclosures, so it cannot descend from them. Common itself is Latin communis via Anglo-Norman; the legal sense of common as a right is not tested here.
Etymology: Legal sense = rights not land; the modern sense "ordinary, low" is enclosure's contempt. Project struck: disparaging from c.1300.

Note: Commoner is common plus -er, and common is Latin communis, com- plus munis. Wiktionary traces munis to a root meaning to exchange; it does not give the 'bound by shared obligation' reading, so treat that as interpretation.
Etymology: From common, L. communis (shared by all, general) — com- (together) + munis (bound, obligated; same root as municipal, immune). The buried sense is not "ordinary person" but "one bound together with others under a shared obligation."

Note: Middle English complexion meant temperament, from Medieval Latin complexio, constitution: the balance of humours, not skin colour.
Etymology: Originally humoral balance, not skin colour.

Note: Wiktionary has cop as an obsolete word for a top or summit, especially of a hill, quoted from 1622. Whether Old Cople Lane comes from it is untested.
Etymology: Old Cople Lane: etymology uncertain, possibly Old English copp (summit).

Note: Wiktionary calls it probably from Romani košter, a stick. It gives no date, so the 19th-century dating needs checking. For the consultant.
Etymology: Bludgeon; 19th century; possibly Romani.

Note: Wiktionary derives cotton from Arabic quṭun via Italian and French, and has no sense of napped wool. It does record a separate verb 'to cotton', to agree, from c.1560s, possibly Welsh. The wool claim needs a period source.
Etymology: In this period meant a napped wool, not the plant fibre; true cotton affordable only after the 1760s.

Note: Old English cræft meant strength and skill, from a Germanic word for power, the same one behind German Kraft. Virtue later took over its sense of power.
Etymology: Craft degraded where German Kraft (strength, power) did not: the older English sense was strength, power.

Note: No dictionary entry for the name; crooked itself is Middle English croked, bent. A place-name dictionary is needed.
Etymology: Croxted Lane = "crooked street".

Note: From Old English cunnende, knowing how, from cunnan, to know. Wiktionary confirms the knowledge root; the cunning man and the later sneer are not dated.
Etymology: The cunning man was a folk healer; the pejorative-only sense is later.

Note: Wiktionary derives cushy from Hindustani khushi, happiness, from Persian, not from Romani. Romani kushti, good, is a different word; Wiktionary suggests cushy may in turn have influenced cushty.
Etymology: Project struck "from Romani"; Hindi khush (pleasant), 1915.

Note: Wiktionary has daj, mother, in Romani and Welsh Romani, comparing Hindi dādī and dāī. It does not give Sanskrit dhāya, and it does not date the word in English Romani. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: mother, from Sanskrit dhāya.

Note: Data is Latin for things given, the plural of datum; base comes from Latin basis, from Greek. Literally a footing of given things.
Etymology: data (L. datum, "something given") + base (L. basis, "foundation, stepping place") — literally a foundation of given things. The word assumes knowledge is something you give once and then stand on reliably, rather than rebuild each time.

Note: Deal is Old English dǣlan, to divide or share out, beside the noun dǣl, a part. German Teil is a cognate and dole is related, so the oldest deal is a share-out, not a bargain.
Etymology: OE dālan, "to divide, share out, distribute" — same root as dole and German teilen. The oldest sense isn't transaction at all but division of a common store among a group.

Note: Defer meaning put off is a variant of differ, from Latin differre, to carry apart. Defer meaning yield to someone is a separate word, from Latin deferre.
Etymology: L. differre, dis- (apart) + ferre (to carry, bear). The original sense is spatial: to carry something away, to put at a distance. A deferred claim carries the assertion away from the point of utterance and deposits it somewhere else — in the reader's assembly of detail.

Note: Via Middle French from Italian disastro, dis- plus astro, star: ill-starred. The 1590s arrival date is not on the page.
Etymology: Just arrived in the 1590s and still meant ill-starred (from astrology).

Note: Dis- plus enchantment; in the social-science sense Wiktionary calls it a calque of Weber's Entzauberung. Zauber means magic (Duden), while enchant goes back to Latin incantare, to chant: the German loses magic, the English loses song.
Etymology: Weber's Entzauberung = "de-magicking" from Zauber (magic); English "enchantment" is from Latin incantare "to sing upon"; so the English names loss of singing.

Note: From Anglo-Norman dismal, Old French dis mals, the bad days, from Medieval Latin dies mali. The unlucky calendar days came first; the gloom followed.
Etymology: From dies mali (Egyptian Days), the 24 unlucky days of the medieval calendar.

Note: Wiktionary traces document via Middle French to Latin documentum and gives a paper used as proof or support. It gives no sense history, so the claim that the 17th-century word meant the evidence rather than the paper is untested.
Etymology: In the 17th century meant evidence or proof, not the paper itself.

Note: Wiktionary glosses Romani drabarni as a witch or sorceress, from drabarel, to bewitch, and traces it to Sanskrit darbha, sacred grass, not to drab, medicine. The healer sense may still hold in English Romani; ask before using it for Jem's mother. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: a healer or herbalist (from drab, medicine, herb).

Note: Middle English drift, an act of driving or a drove, from the same root as drive. German Trift still means a drove or a pasture.
Etymology: The same word as drove/drāf in its older sense: a body of animals moving together.

Note: Romani drom, way or road, is a loan from Medieval Greek dromos, not an Indic word. Dates in English Romani are not tested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: road, from Greek dromos.

Note: Old English drāf, a driving, a herd, and even the road cattle were driven along; drive comes from the same root and a drover is drove plus -er. The early-13th-century place-name date is not tested.
Etymology: drove/drover: as a place-name element traceable to the early 13th century (Drove End, Drove Lane); 'drive' is from the same root; drover from Old English drāf, 'a driving, a herd being driven'.

Note: Wiktionary has dukkeripen as a fortune told by a fortune-teller, with no etymology and no date. Nothing supports a 17th-century attestation. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: fortune-telling (dukkeripen; dukkering, from dukker, to tell fortunes); claimed attested by the 17th century. Seed: no record before the 19th century.

Note: Earn is Old English earnian. Wiktionary says the Germanic verb was formed from a noun meaning harvest, so earning began as reaping.
Etymology: OE earnian, "to deserve, merit, win by labour or service" — related to Gothic asans, "harvest, harvest-time." The oldest sense is agricultural: earning was tied to the labour of a season producing its yield.

Note: Wiktionary gives egad as a softened 'by God', not 'oh God'.
Etymology: Oath, from "Oh God" / "a God".

Note: Old English eldra or ieldra is the comparative of eald, old. An elder is simply an older one.
Etymology: OE ieldra, comparative of eald (old) — literally "more old." Never meant simply "aged"; carried authority by default, the comparative form doing double duty as social rank (church elder, tribal elder).

Note: Latin emendare, to free from fault, from ex- plus mendum, a blemish, via Middle English emenden. Emend and amend are the same Latin verb; emend came straight from Latin. Wiktionary gives no date, so c.1400 needs Etymonline.
From Middle French emotion, from Latin emovere, to move out or stir up. That fits the public-disturbance sense, but the 1650s date is not on the page.
Etymology: "Inner feeling" from the 1650s; earlier a public disturbance.

Note: From Old French enchanter, from Latin incantare, and a twin of incant. Wiktionary does not spell out 'sing upon' or date the senses.
Etymology: Latin incantare, in- + cantare, to sing upon; figurative "delight" sense from the late 14th c.; enchantment as allurement 1670s.

Note: Duden gives Entzauberung as the act of disenchanting, and Zauber as a magical act, spell or charm, of unknown origin. So Weber's word means taking the magic out.
Etymology: German: Weber's term, literally the de-magicking of the world, from Zauber, magic or spell.

Note: Essay arrives in the late 16th century from Middle French essai, a trial or attempt, in the sense Montaigne had just given it. Behind it is Latin exagium, a weighing.
Etymology: From French essai = attempt or trial; Montaigne's form.

Note: From Old French estover. Wiktionary glosses it as obligation, close to but not the same as 'that which is necessary'.
Etymology: The right to take necessary wood; from Old French estover, "that which is necessary".

Note: Ethnicity is ethnic plus -ity. Ethnic comes via Latin ethnicus, heathen, from Greek ethnos, first a company or band, later a people. The heathen sense supports the outsiders point; the bees and the Septuagint are not on the page.
Etymology: Ethnicity, from Greek ethnos — which first meant simply a band living together, a company, even a swarm of bees. It only became a word about identity when the Septuagint translators used it for goyim, the nations — meaning the other nations, the not-us. So the word we use for our own people acquired its force from being applied by outsiders to strangers. You cannot say "my ethnicity" without using a word built from someone else's vantage point — which is the archive problem again, wearing different clothes.

Note: Via Old French and Latin from Greek etumologia, from etumon, the true sense, and -logia, study. Wiktionary gives no dates for the late 14th century or the 1640s discipline.
Etymology: Late 14th century; the modern discipline from the 1640s.

Note: From Latin evidentia, clearness (in Late Latin, a proof), a word Cicero coined from evidens, plain to see.
Etymology: From Latin evidentia, ex- + videre, "seeing out": that which is plainly visible; it never meant trace or residue.

Note: From Latin excruciare, ex- plus cruciare, to torture, from crux, cross. Wiktionary quotes excruciate from c.1587–88, so it was current in 1589.
Etymology: Means crucified: Latin excruciare, ex- + cruciare "to torment", from crux "cross"; arrives in English in the 16th century as a metaphor for extreme pain.

Note: From Anglo-Norman extente, a valuation of land, from extendre, to stretch out. The writ named in the doc is not on the page, but the valuation sense is.
Etymology: From Latin extendere, to stretch out; in English law a valuation survey of land, from the writ extendi facias "cause to be valued"; the mere-size sense is the later ghost.

Note: Law Latin felo de se, a felon of himself: suicide as a crime against oneself.
Etymology: Legal term for suicide: self-murder, a felony against the self, with forfeiture and denial of Christian burial.

Note: Forest comes from medieval Latin forestis, perhaps from foris, outside: the wood outside. Wiktionary offers that beside a Germanic origin and says nothing about 'outside the common law'; the legal meaning is history, not the root.
Etymology: In medieval law, land outside (Latin foris) the common law, reserved for the king's hunting; not necessarily woodland.

Note: Wiktionary glosses Old English forhēawan as to slaughter or cut down. 'Beyond recovery' is the intensifying for- read into it, not a gloss on the page.
Etymology: Old English "hewn utterly, hewn beyond recovery", with the intensifying for- prefix (Kingsnorth).

Note: Duden gives Middle High German vorst, Old High German forst, origin unknown, meaning managed and bounded woodland. It says nothing about an original hunting-law sense.
Etymology: German Forst, like English forest, was originally a legal term (land under the lord's hunting law), not an ecological one.

Note: A minced form of God's hooks: the nails of the crucifixion.
Etymology: Oath, from "God's hooks".

Note: Wiktionary gives galdor as a form of Old English ġealdor and galan as to sing or to enchant. The double sense of song and spell is in the verb.
Etymology: Old English galdor meant both song and spell, from galan "to sing".

Note: Duden gives Middle High German gemeinschaft and Old High German gimeinscaf, community. The comparison with English 'common' is interpretation a dictionary cannot test.
Etymology: German Gemeinschaft kept its full communal charge while English "common" slid toward "vulgar".

Note: Wiktionary confirms glamour is a Scots alteration of grammar, meaning magic, and a twin of grimoire and gramarye. The 1720 Allan Ramsay date, Scott in 1805 and the 1840 shift to beauty are not on the page; check them on Etymonline. Not in 1589.
Etymology: Scots alteration of grammar; first attested c.1720 (Allan Ramsay) meaning magic spell; Scott popularised it 1805; attractiveness sense c.1840. Did not exist in 1589.

Note: Wiktionary treats gorger, Gorgio and gadjo as forms of one Romani word for a non-Romani person, and glosses Gorgio as a Romani term for a house-dweller. Dates are not tested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: non-Romani person (gorjer/gorja/gadjo).

Note: Gospel is Old English godspell, God plus spell, the message of God. Wiktionary says it was probably reshaped from an earlier good-spell, good news, a translation of Greek euangelion.
Etymology: Old English gōd-spell = good story, good news.

Note: Grammar comes from Old French gramaire, learning, from Latin grammatica and Greek grammatikē, skill in letters. Wiktionary's grimoire entry shows Old French gramaire already meant grammar, a book of spells and a magician. The 12th-century date is not on the page.
Etymology: Latin grammatica from Greek grammatikē, art of letters; Old French gramaire (12th c.) already meant both learning and magic incantation.

Note: Grand- plus pa, after grandfather. Wiktionary gives no date, so whether it suits a Penge woman in 1889 is untested.
Etymology: Register check from a draft Telling: is "grandpa" the right word for a working woman in Penge in 1889?

Note: French grimoire is a variant of grammaire, so a spell book is literally a grammar. The 1849 date of its arrival in English is not on the page.
Etymology: The same word as grammar/glamour again; entered English from French in 1849.

Note: Wiktionary derives grimy from grime plus -y, and grime from Middle English grim, soot on the face, from Old English grīma, a mask, probably reinforced by Dutch. Nothing links it to the Grimes family of Croydon colliers: keep that as a story people tell, not an etymology.
Etymology: May derive from the Grimes family of Croydon colliers (Francis Grimes, 16th c.). Project struck: grime 1580s, grimy 1610s.

Note: A clipping of Gyptian, from Egyptian, because the Roma were wrongly thought to come from Egypt when they reached England in the 16th century. Spanish gitano has the same origin. For the consultant.
Etymology: From 'Egyptian': the legal classification of the Egyptians Acts calcified into place names (Gipsy Hill, named from long-standing encampments). Egyptian was the Tudor statute word for Romani people.

Note: From Old French hanter, to inhabit or frequent, from Old Norse or Old English words meaning to bring home, from the Germanic word for home. A haunt is where you live. The date of the ghostly sense is not on the page.
Etymology: Old French hanter, to frequent; a haunt was your usual ground; the ghostly sense attaches only in the late 16th century.

Note: Old English hāligdæġ, holy day or Sabbath. The date of the secular-leisure sense is not on the page.
Etymology: "Holiday" is holy day; the secular-leisure sense not fully established until the 19th century.

Note: Hostile is Latin hostilis, from hostis, enemy. Wiktionary's Latin entry cites Varro saying hostis once meant a stranger, and its root also gave English guest.
Etymology: L. hostilis, from hostis — originally simply "stranger, foreigner," and only later "enemy." The semantic drift from outsider to enemy happened inside the word itself.

Note: From Latin ūmor, liquid; Wiktionary says the four bodily humours gave the sense mood, and mood narrowed to wit. The h is a folk-etymology from humus. The 1680s date is not on the page.
Etymology: "Funny" sense from the 1680s; earlier a bodily fluid.

Note: Old English hyrst, a hillock, a wood or a wooded rise; German Horst is a cousin. Selhurst carries it.
Etymology: The -hurst suffix (Selhurst) = wooded hill.

Note: From Anglo-Norman emprouwer, from en- plus prou, profit: to turn to profit. The 1610s date for 'make better' is not on the page.
Etymology: From Anglo-French emprouwer, "to turn to profit"; the "make better" sense only from the 1610s.

Note: Latin index meant an informer, a pointer and the forefinger, from indicare, to point out. The finger came before the list.
Etymology: L. index, "one who points out, discloser, informer" — from in- (toward) + dicere (to say, point out). The oldest sense isn't a list at all; it's a finger pointing. An index doesn't contain the knowledge — it gestures at where the knowledge lives.

Note: From Medieval Latin influentia, a flowing in. Wiktionary keeps an astrological sense, a force from the stars shaping a person's character. The ethereal fluid and the dating of the shift to social power are not on the page.
Etymology: Originally astrological: an ethereal fluid flowing from the stars into bodies; social-power sense is later.

Note: From Latin invenire, to come upon or find, in- plus venire, to come. The finding sense is confirmed; the date of the fabricating sense is not on the page.
Etymology: Originally meant to find: Latin invenire, in- + venire "to come upon"; the Invention of the Cross is its finding; the fabrication sense takes hold in the 16th century.

Note: From the minced oath 'by jingo' in G. W. Hunt's music-hall song of about 1878, backing a belligerent line on Russia. Jingo itself is a euphemism for Jesus.
Etymology: Jingoism, reflexive belligerent patriotism, derives from a music-hall song of 1878: 'We don't want to fight, but by jingo if we do...'

Note: Wiktionary gives cushty (spelled kushti too) as from Romani kushto or kushti, good. Its earliest quotation is from 1937, and nothing on the page supports a 17th-century date; the project's own correction says no record before the 19th century. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: good; claimed attested in English Romani by the 17th century. Seed: no record before the 19th century.

Note: German Köhler, a charcoal burner (Wiktionary); also a surname.
Etymology: German: charcoal burner; the man of the Meiler.

Note: Duden gives blind faith, and traces it to an old story of a collier who, asked about his faith, gave a strikingly simple answer. Proverbial contempt for colliers' minds is the doc's gloss, not Duden's.
Etymology: Köhlerglauben: German for blind faith, literally charcoal-burner's faith, from the collier's proverbial credulity.

Note: Old English hlāfmæsse, loaf-mass, the harvest festival on 1 August.
Etymology: Lammas (1 August) is "loaf-mass": the first grain offered at church.

Note: Ledger is Middle English liggere, from liggen, a form of lie: to lie still, to stay in place. The stay-put idea holds, but the root is lie, not lay, and Dutch legger is a cousin, not the route in.
Etymology: Ledger — from Middle English leggen, to lay, via Dutch legger: the book that lies permanently in one place, as against the books that travelled. A ledger was defined by its immobility before it was defined by its contents — the record that stays put while the people recorded in it are moved through. The Anerley registers were ledgers in both senses: they lay in the board-room for eighty years, and every child in them was in transit.

Note: From Late Latin legibilis, readable, from legere. Wiktionary's page does not gloss legere as to gather or choose. Literate is a separate root (see its row).
Etymology: Latin legere, to read, originally to gather, pick out, choose (also elect, select, collect, intelligence = inter + legere).

Note: From Latin litteratus, lettered, from littera, a letter, so it is unrelated to legible. It pushed out Old English stæfwīs, letter-wise.
Etymology: Latin littera, a letter; unrelated root to legible.

Note: Lunch existed by 1580 but meant a hunk or lump; the meal sense dates from 1829. Luncheon as a light meal is attested from 1652, so it is available in 1689 where lunch is not.
Etymology: "Lunch" did not exist in 1689; a possible afternoon snack was a "nuncheon".

Note: Wiktionary gives manifest from Latin manifestus, palpable, from manus, hand, plus an uncertain element. It says nothing about the ship's cargo-list sense or 1706.
Etymology: Ship's cargo list sense, 1706.

Note: The oath marry is the Virgin's name, from Middle English Marie. It has nothing to do with marrying, which comes from Latin maritare.
Etymology: Oath, "by the Virgin Mary".

Note: Duden and Wiktionary both derive Meiler from Medieval Latin miliarium, a quantity of a thousand pieces, after the many stacked billets, from mille, thousand. 'Milestone' is wrong; the Meiler that comes from mile is a different word, a runner of the mile.
Etymology: Doc 19 derives it from Latin miliarium, "milestone" (the mound resembled a stone column). Project struck the gloss: Duden gives a pile of about a thousand billets.

Note: No Wiktionary entry under meripen or meriben, so the Sanskrit derivation and the date are untested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: death, from Sanskrit mṛ-.

Note: Short for mobile, from Latin mobile vulgus, the fickle crowd. Wiktionary gives no date for it, so the 1680s needs Etymonline.
Etymology: 1680s, clipped from mobile vulgus (the fickle crowd).

Note: Mobile plus phone; mobile is Latin mobilis, easy to move. Wiktionary gives no date, so 'by 1983' needs Etymonline.
No Wiktionary entry under mochadi, mokhadi, mochardi or mokadi. Okely remains the source; this is a word to take to the consultant, not to a dictionary. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: ritually unclean, polluted; the purity system (Okely).

Note: Navvy is a clipping of navigator, from the navigation canals the first navvies dug. A word for someone who steers a ship became the word for the man with the spade.
Etymology: Navvy, the men who cut it, is a clipping of navigator — from Latin navis, ship, and agere, to drive. Canals were "navigations," so the men who dug them were navigators. A word for someone who steers a vessel across open water, transferred to the man with the shovel who makes the water in the first place — and applied, on this ground, to work that consisted of cutting a common in half.

Note: The verse read to claim benefit of clergy, said to be the first verse of Psalm 51. Wiktionary quotes it from 1619.
Etymology: Psalm 51 read in Latin to claim benefit of clergy and escape hanging; reading test abolished 1706.

Note: Old English nēahġebūr, literally near-dweller: nigh plus ġebūr, a dweller or farmer. There is no warmth in it, only distance.
Etymology: OE nēahgebūr, from nēah (near) + gebūr (dweller, farmer — same root as boor, German Bauer). Originally meant nothing sentimental — just "the farmer who lives near." The social weight of "neighbourliness" was built onto a word that started as pure geography.

Note: From Old French nice, simple or foolish, from Latin nescius, ignorant. Wiktionary dates 'fastidious' and 'scrupulous' from the 14th century, 'foolish' 14th–17th, and 'pleasant' only from the 18th.
Etymology: "Pleasant" sense from 1769; in 1589 it meant precise, fastidious.

Note: Old English nihtegale, night-singer, from night plus gale, to sing; the n before g was added later.
Etymology: From Old English galan, to sing (night-singer).

Note: Wiktionary gives normalise as normal plus -ise, an English formation, with no date and no French borrowing. The 1860s date needs Etymonline.
Etymology: Did not enter English until the 1860s, borrowed from French.

Note: North plus wood. The claim that 'Great North Wood' dates only from 1898 is not tested by this source.
Etymology: Simply "north wood", from Croydon's perspective; "Great North Wood" was coined only in 1898.

Note: Coined in 1688 by the physician Johannes Hofer from Greek nostos, return home, and algos, pain, as a learned version of German Heimweh. The word is brand new in the 1689 book and absent in 1589.
Etymology: Coined 1688 by Swiss physician Johannes Hofer from Gk nostos (return home) + algos (pain) — literally "the pain of returning home," first used as a clinical diagnosis for homesick soldiers, believed capable of killing them. The word didn't exist yet in 1589.

Note: Middle English nonshench, a light refreshment usually taken in the afternoon, from noon plus shench, a drink poured out.
Etymology: A light afternoon snack; the word in use in 1689 where "lunch" was not.

Note: Via Old French from Latin oraculum, and Wiktionary's first sense is a shrine of a prophetic god: a place. The link to orare and os, mouth, is not on the page.
Etymology: From Latin orare, to speak or plead (as oration, orator), ultimately from os, mouth; originally a speaking place where a god answered.

Note: Wiktionary defines an orphan as someone who has lost both parents, or more rarely one. It gives no special 'fatherless' sense for the 17th century; the project traced that usage to the City of London's Court of Orphans. The word comes from Greek orphanos via Late Latin.
Etymology: In the 17th century meant a child whose father had died, not both parents. Project struck: that was the City's Court of Orphans usage.

Note: From Angloromani pal, brother or friend, from Romani phral, brother, from Sanskrit; English brother is a distant cousin. Wiktionary gives no date, so the 1680s needs checking. For the consultant.
Etymology: From Romani phral (brother); in English from the 1680s.

Note: Wiktionary has the thieves' cant word as pannum, bread or food, probably from Latin panem or Italian pane. Its earliest quotation shown is Brome, 1641–42; the Harman 1567 date is not on the page.
Etymology: Thieves' cant for bread, Harman 1567.

Note: Romani pani, water, inherited from Prakrit and ultimately Sanskrit pānīya. Wiktionary also lists it in Angloromani, Welsh Romani and even Scots. Dates in English Romani are not tested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: water, from Sanskrit pānīya.

Note: Via French from Latin parallelus, from Greek. Wiktionary points to para-, beside, and allo-, other, without spelling out the 'one another' gloss.
Etymology: Gk para- (beside) + allelos (one another) — lines that run beside each other without ever meeting. A parallel structure doesn't converge to a single point of meaning; it holds two things in alignment without resolving them into one.

Note: From Latin passio, suffering, from pati, to suffer. The sequence of senses and their dates are not on the page.
Etymology: Latin passio "suffering"; c.1200 only the sufferings of Christ; "strong emotion" mid-13th c.; "sexual love" by the 1580s.

Note: Pencil first meant a fine paintbrush, from Old French pincil and Latin penicillum, a little tail; it is not related to pen. The brush sense runs from the 14th century to at least 1603, but the source does not test what a writer would have meant in 1689.
Etymology: In 1689 could mean a fine artist's brush or the newer graphite black-lead pencil.

Note: Wiktionary has Penge only as a place, with no etymology. Doc 35 cites Gover, Mawer and Stenton, The Place-Names of Surrey (1934), for pen plus coed; check that book or the Key to English Place-Names.
Etymology: One of London's few surviving Celtic place names: Brythonic pen (head, edge) + coed (wood) = edge of the wood (Doc 02) or "top of the wood" (Doc 21); Welsh cognate Pencoed; 957 charter "Pænge"; 1067 Penceat.

Note: Latin potens, able or powerful, the present participle of posse, to be able, from potis, which originally meant a lord or master.
Etymology: L. potens, from potentia (power, ability) — literally "capable, able to do." Not about emotion or sentiment, but about power: the capacity to do something, to mean something, to have force.

Note: Latin proiectus, thrown forth, from proicere.
Etymology: L. projectus, past participle of proicere (to throw forward) — pro- (forward) + icere (to throw). A project is something thrown forward into time, held together across multiple moments.

Note: Old English rǣdan meant to counsel, advise or interpret as well as to read, from a Germanic verb meaning to advise. To read was to make sense of something, not only of letters.
Etymology: Old English rædan "to advise, counsel, interpret"; other Germanic cognates still mean advise.

Note: Via Old French recorder from Latin recordari, to call to mind, from re- plus cor, heart. To record was to get something by heart.
Etymology: Latin recordari, re- + cor "heart": to record was to learn by heart.

Note: Via French from Old French resourse, a spring, from resourdre, to rise again (Latin resurgere). A resource is a source that keeps rising.
Etymology: OF resourse, from resourdre (to rise again, spring up) — literally "a rising again." A resource is something you can return to, that supplies something anew each time you use it.

Note: From Latin retortus, from retorquere, to twist back.
Etymology: From Latin retortus, "twisted back"; the airtight vessel that replaced the clamp.

Note: Wiktionary has Romani rukh, tree, from Prakrit rukkha, from Sanskrit rukṣa or vṛkṣa. Dates in English Romani are not tested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: tree, from Sanskrit rukṣa/vṛkṣa.

Note: Secret is Latin secretus, separated or hidden, from secernere, to set apart. Secrecy is a later English reshaping of Middle English secretee.
Etymology: L. secretus, past participle of secernere (to separate, set apart) — se- (apart) + cernere (to sift, distinguish). The root sense is not concealment but separation-by-sifting: a secret is a thing sorted out from the general mass and set to one side.

Note: Old English sǣd, that which is sown, from a root meaning to sow: confirmed. The row's link to Gothic asans, harvest, is a slip: that belongs to earn, which has a different root.
Etymology: OE sǻd, from the same Germanic root as sow — literally "that which is sown." Related to Gothic asans, "harvest, harvest-time." A seeded database, like seeded ground, only produces something if what's planted is left to grow.

Note: Old English scrūd, a garment, is confirmed, and Wiktionary lists the burial cloth and the mast ropes as senses of one word. So they are not unrelated, as the row's first sentence says; the rest of the row stands.
Etymology: The rigging term is unrelated to the burial sense — from Old English scrud, "garment, clothing," the ropes conceived as dressing the mast. The burial "shroud" is the same root, a garment for the last dressing of the body. A single Old English word for "what clothes a thing" ended up naming both what keeps a ship upright and what covers the dead. The coincidence sits unremarked in a building full of pauper children being dressed for the sea — one word for the rigging they're being trained to use and the grave-cloth that will dress them after the North Sea does its work. Maximally resonant to the series' themes of disposal and the navy as an apparatus for sending poor children away.

Note: Old English sǣlig, lucky, and Wiktionary traces the slide lucky, innocent, naive, foolish. It gives no dates, so 'still blessed in 1589' is untested.
Etymology: In 1589 still carried blessed, innocent, vulnerable; foolish is later.

Note: From the Belgian town of Spa and its iron springs. Wiktionary credits Timothy Bright's 'English Spaw' of 1596, at Harrogate, with starting the generic use.
Etymology: A Belgian town's name (Spa) that became a common noun.

Note: Spell the noun is Old English spell, news or story, kept in gospel. Spell the verb came through Anglo-Norman espeler and merged with Old English spellian, to tell. The 1570s and 14th-century dates are not on the page.
Etymology: Old English spell "story, saying" (kept in gospel); magic sense first recorded 1570s (Spenser); "read letter by letter" early 14th c. via Anglo-French espeller.

Note: From Latin spiritus, breath or spirit, from spirare, to breathe. It pushed out Old English gast, which survives as ghost.
Etymology: Breath, vital principle, supernatural being and distilled essence at once; Latin spiritus, breath.

Note: Structure plus -al. Wiktionary says 19th century; the exact year 1821 is not on the page.
From Old French suburbe, Latin suburbium: sub- plus urbs, under or just outside the city. It pushed out Old English underburg. The swing from disreputable to aspirational is not in the source.
Etymology: Latin suburbium = "under the city", at the city's edge; faintly disreputable in the 17th century, aspirational by 1889.

Note: Suffrage plus -ette, first used by the Daily Mail in 1906 as a sneer, then taken up by the WSPU itself. The page does not address whether men could be called suffragettes; suffragist is the broader word.
Etymology: suffragette denotes a woman of the militant WSPU; a man could not be a suffragette; suffragist is the broader term.

Note: From Anglo-Norman tallie, a notched stick recording a debt, from Latin talea, a cut rod. Wiktionary does not call it unrelated to tell; it even invites comparison with the Germanic word for number, so treat 'unrelated' as likely, not settled.
Etymology: Latin talea, a cut stick, via Anglo-Norman; unrelated to tell (tellan) despite the resemblance.

Note: Tell is Old English tellan, to count or to tell, from a Germanic word for number, and tale shares the root. A bank teller and 'all told' still count.
Etymology: OE tellan, "to count, enumerate, relate, narrate." Same root as tale and talk, but buried deeper is number — to tell is originally to count, to make a reckoning. A Telling is literally a counting-out. The arithmetical sense survives in "it tells" (it matters, it weighs in the account).

Note: From Latin temperare, to divide or mix in due proportion, linked to tempus, the fit season. One word for balancing metal, humours and moods.
Etymology: Latin temperare "to mix in due proportion": metal, humours and disposition at once.

Note: Via Old French from Latin textus, style or texture, from texere, to weave. Text and texture are the same word.
Etymology: Latin textus "something woven", from texere, to weave.

Note: Old English þrǣd, from a root meaning to rub or twist. Throw, Old English þrāwan, to turn or twist, comes from the same root.
Etymology: Thread, from Old English þrǣd, related to þrāwan, to twist or turn — the same root gives throw. A thread was originally the thing produced by throwing fibre into a spin. Which is a fair description of what's happening across these sessions: nothing here is a new fact so much as an old fact given a twist that lets it catch on another one.

Note: Middle English turnpyke, a spiked barrier across a road, first used to block a road until a toll was paid. Wiktionary does not mention cavalry; the barrier and the toll are confirmed.
Etymology: A pike set in a turning frame, a spiked barrier against cavalry; then the tollgate; then the road.

Note: Angloromani vardo, from Romani vordon, a borrowing from Iranian, from a root meaning to turn. The mid-19th-century date for the wagon is not tested here. For the consultant.
Etymology: The Romani decorated wagon; the word and object did not emerge until the mid-19th century (post-1850s).

Note: From Latin versus, a line of writing and originally a row or furrow, from vertere, to turn. The ploughman's turn at the end of the furrow is the poet's line-break.
Etymology: Latin versus "a turning of the plough".

Note: Wiktionary gives Romani veś, forest, as a borrowing from Iranian (compare Persian bêše), not from Sanskrit vṛkṣa. Vesh is its anglicised spelling. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: forest, wood, from Sanskrit vṛkṣa.

Note: No Wiktionary entry. The parts are attested: veś, forest, and the agent suffix -engro, but the compound and its date are untested. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: forester/woodman (vesh + -engro). Seed: no record before the 19th century.

Note: Villain and villein are doublets from Late Latin villanus, a peasant bound to a villa, via Old French vilein. The moral sense came later.
Etymology: villain and villein are the same word: Latin villa, a farmhouse, via Old French vilain, a person attached to the villa, a farm labourer; the moral sense is a later imposition by the class that owned the villas.

Note: Latin virtus, manliness or worth, from vir, man. Wiktionary records the sense 'inherent power or efficacy' from the 13th century, so a herb's virtue was its working force. Virtue also pushed out Old English cræft, which survives as craft.
Etymology: Latin virtus "strength, power, manliness" from vir "man"; herbs had virtue (healing power).

Note: Wiktionary dates wastrel to 1847 and builds it from waste plus the pejorative suffix -rel, so it was an insult from its first record. Nothing shows it ever meaning a commoner or a person of the waste. The project's own note says 1790; settle the date on Etymonline.
Etymology: A person of the waste (the common) = a commoner; became an insult only after enclosure. Project struck: waste + -rel, from 1790.

Note: Watch is Old English wæċċan, to stay awake; its cousins German wecken and Swedish väcka mean to wake someone.
Etymology: OE wæccan (to wake, keep watch, be vigilant). Carries the sense of one awake while others sleep, alert to what moves. Used across Middle English for sentries, guardians, vigilant observers. By the sixteenth century increasingly marked as a profession, but retains the older sense of attentiveness, not just presence.

Note: The compound is older than the row says: Old English weorchūs meant a workshop. The poor-law sense came later, and Wiktionary gives no date for it, so check the 17th-century date on Etymonline.
Etymology: Compound of work (OE) + house (OE), first recorded in the 17th century as a plain descriptive: a house where the poor were set to work. But by the 1834 New Poor Law the word had drifted from description to euphemism. The institutions built after 1834 were designed to be feared, not merely to house labour, and "workhouse" survived as the name anyway, carrying its older, softer sense as camouflage over a harder new function. The word performed substitution in real time: an old name kept its power to obscure while the reality beneath it transformed. A precise instance of how records substitute a legible thing (the name) for a true thing (the function).

Note: Old English wrītan, from a Germanic verb meaning to carve or write, from a root meaning to tear. Writing began as scratching.
Etymology: Old English writan "to scratch, carve, cut".

Note: Wiktionary lists the Romani word as jag, fire, inherited from a Prakrit form aggi. It does not test the Sanskrit agni step or when the word is first recorded in English Romani. For the consultant.
Etymology: Romani: fire, from Sanskrit agni; attested in English Romani by the 17th century.

Note: A minced form of God's wounds, the wounds of the crucifixion.
Etymology: Oath, from "God's wounds".
